extracted.intended_audience: regulators, regulatory lawyers, CRTC staff, broadcasters, telecommunications companies, and public interest interveners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards governing public notice, hearing formats, policy development, interveners' costs, and disclosure of information in CRTC broadcasting and telecommunications proceedings. Focuses on how the CRTC should inform, involve, and treat members of the public and interveners, and how it balances confidentiality and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of administrative tribunal before appellate courts
rubrics_metrics.description: A board may appear as a party and make representations but only as to matters relating to its jurisdiction; questions of jurisdiction do not include the issue of whether or not the board has contravened the rules of natural justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have limited the role of an administrative tribunal whose decision is under review to an explanatory role with reference to the record and to making representations relating to jurisdiction. Tribunals should not debate issues of natural justice as protagonists before the appellate court; such issues should be fought out by the parties. Allowing a tribunal to vindicate itself risks producing a spectacle 'not ordinarily contemplated in our judicial traditions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative provision for CRTC to be heard on jurisdictional challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: It is recommended that a specific provision granting the CRTC the right to be heard on appeals to challenge its jurisdiction, including allegations that it has exceeded its jurisdiction by breaching natural justice, should be provided by legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National Transportation Act grants this right for telecommunications appeals but Broadcasting Act lacks a similar specific right; providing it would allow the CRTC to continue to be heard on jurisdictional challenges for reasons of institutional necessity and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice — broadcasting announcement requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish announcements in the Canada Gazette and local newspapers and broadcast them over any radio or television station to which the application relates; rules require four announcements informing the public of the date fixed for the hearing, the nature of the matter, and the rights of interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission's working paper suggests increasing the number of broadcast notices for licence renewals to as many as 20 and for other types of applications to as many as 16. Such announcements should also give notice of any decisions following the hearing that amend licences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast licence-term public-accountability notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Require licensees to broadcast notices during the currency of their licence terms at least twice a month stating they make use of radio frequencies which are public property, that their undertakings must be operated in the public interest, that the licensee welcomes comment and criticism, and that its public file is available during business hours for public viewing at the station's offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is proposed to enhance ongoing public awareness and accountability of licensees beyond single-application notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telecommunications notice by billing insert
rubrics_metrics.description: For general rate increases and similar matters, notices should be mailed to each telephone subscriber as part of the monthly billing and include a brief description of the application, how the subscriber's rates would be affected, a detailed schedule of proposed changes, reasons for the increase, and explicit instructions on how subscribers can view the application and comment or intervene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This billing-insert innovation increased public response dramatically in early telephone rate applications and is proposed to be extended to cable operator rate-change applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register of 'interested parties' service
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow any person to register with the Secretary of the Commission as an 'interested party' for categories of applications (new/amended tariffs, general rate increases, interconnection agreements, capital issues); after registration such persons must be served with all application material at the time it is filed and receive a covering letter describing the application and filing details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules include forms with required content. This register is an innovative procedural notice device in the Telecommunications Rules to ensure timely service of filings to interested stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing public reaction to decide whether to hold hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the nature of an application makes it unclear whether a hearing should be called, publish notice of the application and invite public comment; the Commission then decides, based on comments received, whether to hold a hearing or decide on written documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method has been used in both broadcasting and telecommunications. Wide circulation of such notices had been supported by the Commission's mailing list (later discontinued), which affected the effectiveness of this procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing formats to encourage public participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two types of public hearing formats: (1) a main hearing structured for presentation of applications and interventions, and (2) a town-hall meeting format permitting members of the public to appear on short notice and 'sound off' on matters such as rate issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional hearings for general rate increases are held in communities selected mainly on the basis of where the most written representations originate, usually in the evening to accommodate working persons. The Broadcasting Rules permit community groups to make representations at the main hearing upon 48 hours' notice. These formats help resolve subscriber problems and foster direct access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy development through white papers, briefs, and issue hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop major policies by releasing white papers, calling for written briefs on proposals, and holding public hearings where authors of briefs can appear; use 'issue hearings' to extract recurring topics from rate hearings and treat them as general policy questions by preparing documents, raising questions, and soliciting comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This evolutionary process (used for cable TV, Canadian content, FM broadcasting) can involve multiple documents and hearings before final policy emerges. Although the Broadcasting Act does not require this process for policy, the Act does require publication in the Canada Gazette and reasonable opportunity to make representations for regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervener costs — factors supporting awarding costs (Challenge Communications)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Challenge Communications v. Bell Canada the Commission found factors supporting costs: (1) case was adversary in nature and applicant achieved its principal goal; (2) applicant effectively represented the entire suppliers' section of the industry; (3) applicant brought to attention a tariff contrary to statute and made a substantial contribution to the Commission's statutory responsibilities; (4) costs incurred represented a strain on applicant's financial resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission held that no single factor standing alone would be compelling but the combined effect justified awarding costs. It ordered costs paid on a solicitor-and-client basis according to the tariff of costs in the Supreme Court of Ontario; the bill was subsequently taxed by the General Counsel of the CRTC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervener costs — draft rules criteria for awarding costs in rate proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed criteria for awarding costs to any intervener: (a) has a substantial interest in outcome or represents interests of a substantial number/class of subscribers; (b) has participated in a responsible way; (c) has contributed to a better understanding of the issues by the Commission; (d) does not have sufficient resources to prosecute its interests adequately, given the financial implications, or requires assistance to represent a group/class of subscribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria were applied in awarding costs to municipal federations and public-interest interveners in major general rate applications. The Commission has tried to confine awards to specialized situations deserving of costs, but has broadened its approach in some cases (e.g., ordering applicants to pay costs of CRTC consultants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Awarding costs for CRTC-hired consultants' work
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission has required applicants (e.g., Bell Canada, British Columbia Telephone Company) in certain long-distance rate applications to pay the costs of consultants hired by the CRTC to organize, analyse and report on evidence in hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice was noted as an indication of the scope of the Commission's interpretation of its power to award costs under section 73 of the National Transportation Act and has been the subject of appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting disclosure policy — presumption of public disclosure of financial information
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing rules permitted the Commission, at the applicant's request and if in the Commission's opinion the public interest is best served, to treat certain information (including financial statements) as confidential; the Commission changed practice to require that such financial information filed to support cable rate applications would routinely be made public unless the public interest dictated otherwise. Licensees must maintain a public file containing audited financial statements, licence, promise of performance, and correspondence with the CRTC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission proposes to apply the telecommunications test to broadcasting: before information will be treated as confidential the applicant must establish to the satisfaction of the Commission that disclosure will cause specific direct harm that outweighs the benefit of public disclosure. The proposals considerably extend disclosure requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telecommunications statutory confidentiality and Commission's reverse-onus test
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 331 and 334 of the Railway Act provide statutory confidentiality for carrier cost information and other returns, making disclosure the exception; however, the Commission has applied a balancing approach and effectively reversed the onus so that interveners need only state their need for information and the carriers must prove that disclosure would cause specific direct harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission reasons that effective regulation in the public interest depends on the quality of intervener participation and thus interveners should have as much relevant information as possible; a limitation arises only when disclosure would be likely to cause specific direct harm to the company. The test is difficult for carriers to meet because future competitive harm is uncertain; as a result, more information is available in telecommunications proceedings than previously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing test for disclosure vs. confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Commission obtains confidential information relevant to determination of matters before it, it must strike a balance in the public interest between maintaining confidentiality and the requirements of a proper determination of matters under statutory provisions (e.g., Sections 320 and 321 of the Railway Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This balancing leads to a presumption of disclosure where interveners need relevant information, with exceptions only when specific direct harm to the company is proven to outweigh the public interest in disclosure.
